analysis.investment_thesis: Anup Engineering is a fundamentally sound industrial manufacturer, but at P/E 34.8 and P/B 6.36, Mr. Market is demanding a grotesque premium with no margin of safety whatsoever. The Graham Number works out to approximately INR 644 against a market price of INR 2,022 — the stock trades at more than 3x intrinsic value by my calculation.
key_strengths: Consistent earnings over 6 consecutive years with net profit CAGR of 22.4% (2020–2025)
Conservative balance sheet — Debt/Equity of 0.25, and interest coverage of ~28x (EBIT INR 168 Cr vs finance cost INR 6 Cr)
Revenue nearly tripled from INR 245 Cr to INR 733 Cr over 5 years, demonstrating real business growth
key_risks: Valuation is extreme — P/E 34.8 (my limit: 15) and P/B 6.36 (my limit: 1.5) leave zero margin of safety
Operating cash flow turned negative in FY2025 (-INR 7 Cr) despite INR 118 Cr reported net profit — signals severe working capital deterioration
Borrowings jumped from zero to INR 158 Cr while cash evaporated to INR 3 Cr, reversing the historically debt-free status
red_flags: Graham Number ~INR 644 implies stock is priced at 214% premium to intrinsic value
FY2025 free cash flow: -INR 51 Cr — earnings are not converting to cash
Gross margin of only 3.79% is suspiciously low; operating margin of 17.9% suggests material revenue recognition or cost classification questions
analysis.detailed_analysis:
By the strict arithmetic of Security Analysis, this stock fails every primary valuation test. A P/E of 34.8 is more than double my ceiling of 15; a P/B of 6.36 is over four times my preferred maximum of 1.5. Computing the Graham Number — the square root of (22.5 × EPS ~INR 58.5 × BVPS ~INR 316) — yields roughly INR 644. The investor today is being asked to pay INR 2,022, or three times what the assets and proven earnings justify. That is not investing; it is speculation on continued growth, which I cannot value and will not pay for.

What concerns me further is the FY2025 cash flow collapse. Net profit rose to INR 118 Cr, yet operating cash flow was negative INR 7 Cr and free cash flow was negative INR 51 Cr. Working capital appears to have consumed the entire earnings base. Simultaneously, borrowings surged from near-zero to INR 158 Cr while cash fell to INR 3 Cr. The company may be winning contracts faster than it can finance them — a classic capital-trap in project-based industrials. The business itself is creditable; it is sixty years old, exports products, and serves durable end-markets. But a sound business purchased at a foolish price is still a foolish investment.
